text: the thermals are the best aspect of this card. I was able to get one on sale+rebate+shadowlands(which found its way). It runs up to 125w on OC versions up to the 1660 wattage. It was the cheapest solution at the time last year summer. I almost got a single fan 8gb 580 for 160, bout wound up spending the same anyways. Better thermals and less wattage is largely an aspect of thermals overall in a m-atx/budget build. The gpu/psu dying from heat and the voltages they have to run at those temps. If im going to sell a system to someone i cant be manually undervolting and expecting them to not hit reset in afterburner, or default in adrenaline. Id rather the parts be pNp. As well as if im using 4-550w psu, and the relative level of quality among those bronze psus. The only way it wont fry...is if i get 550w vs 4-450w. And ideally a low wattage GPU like a 5500xt or a 1660s. Which at the time costed more 229 and more for better cooling/ram. I wanted a sub 200$ gpu with a 3600 bc they were also around 169$ on sale...now you cant get either of them at a resonable price. Now a 3600 cant even fully utillize a 3070/6700xt level gpu. Thus the psu methodology. Youd want a "nice" psu if you were going to be OC a cpu and runnig a GPU with high mem bandwidth and overall typically any gpu pushing 200W+. From a 12v rail quality, aspect. Budget gpus and stock cpus IMO can get by with bronze so long as the brand is reputable, or its a viable oem/rebrand. But now the "budget" non k intel chips offer that "super" turbo mode via bios with some budget chipsets....intel is finally going the way of AMD LMAO. We have to think back to a time when the e8500/e8400(poormans version) was competing with quad core extreme intel cpus....and amd users were unlocking their duel core phenoms to 4 with concurrent motherboards to compete with their fellow amd gamers, with the at the time nex-gen games. Intel has finally came to force a "wedge" in the 4-8gb 100-400$ gpu market XD. The reckoning is upon all of our wallets

text:
@hokopl  ive been into pc gaming for 21 years & its always the same: hype up some new technology & when it launches its 10-15% better. In 20 years thats all ive seen except there was an Nvidia range that had like 30-40% perf increase about a decade ago or so ago. 

By rebranding im referring to the performance index of the cards & not architecture - cards are made to be slightly faster than the older generation but to leave enough room for existing cards in R&D to slot into - so we always get 10-15% faster cards

This fact does of course not stop the tech world & media from saying each & every week 'the new [some new gpu tech] could mean [some new fancy claim with no evidemce to support it] or 'could [some new card] be the new tech that gamers were waiting for' - always the same theme & after 20 years of this stuff you just get sick of it

I can save everynody time: whatever cards are coming next expect it to be 10-15% faster on average & more expensive than youre willing to pay for that extra 15%

Take a moment to think about all the gimmicks, hype, 'new architecture & process' ive heard in 21 years - its 2019 now & we still have cards struggling to keep 60fps ultra in 1080p 🙂

author: @treefiddy727

text:
@acryion 

 "each 100mhz gives you 1fps"
It obviously depends on the game, the settings in the game, the CPU being used, etc. 

Also the fact that a 5700 XT can reach a whole 400-450mhz (20-24%) above boost with just liquid cooling indicates great overclocking headroom. At stock, my 2080 ti will hit 1860mhz. If I were able to mod the power limit, and increase my core clock by the same amount all the way to 2300mhz with just liquid cooling, I would be ecstatic, but that's unlikely. Thermals and heat output are not the only things holding my gpu back. You can always buy a better cooler if that's limiting you, but in my case, I can't just change the actual die of my gpu. So far from useless.

That being said, it's possible to do 2000-2100mhz on just the air cooler, depending on how good the manufacturer makes it. That's still great overclocking headroom.

text:
At $170 US for the 5500 XT 4GB, IMO the GTX 1650 SUPER is the stronger offering. The performance difference would be largely unnoticeable, but it costs less, uses less power, and has Turing's excellent NVENC if you're looking at hobbyist streaming. The feature set between the two is now broadly similar, though I still prefer AMD's driver stack, it's not like NVIDIA's is bad, it's just preference.

Other reviews have shown the 8GB framebuffer makes largely no difference to 1080p performance, and the RX 570 4GB has been the go to budget 1080p recommendation for ages, so the VRAM thing doesn't do anything to convince me. It's also not that much of a step up to the GTX 1660 SUPER, which offers performance that's generally a tier above the GTX 1650 SUPER and RX 5500 XT.

AMD needs to be more competitive on price. I'm sure they'd like to break the "budget alternative" moniker, but when you rock up late to the party like this, you've got to offer *something*.

The situation is abit more complicated since Ryzen situation is that the single-core situation is now almost on-par with Intel's, and with Ryzen giving Hyperthreading on all front (plus unlocked and abit better coolers help), there are VERY strong value proposition on going AMD instead of Intel since the difference are so close now that extra features are the one clinching the deal (Motherboard, Optane, etc). There are quite a hype on Zen 3/Zen 2+ architecture however Intel potentially will give Hyperthreading back on all their lineups for next-gen along with potentially deeper discount.
